newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Scania says upturn ahead for European truck market.
newsitem.headline: Scania says upturn ahead for European truck market.

text.p: Swedish truckmaker Scania said on Monday that price pressure continued to plague the Western European truck market in the first half of 1997, but said the market seemed to be picking up.
It said orders for trucks rose eight percent in the first six months of the year in Western Europe compared to the year earlier period.
Scania said it expected this improved order intake to have a positive effect on sales in the second half of 1997.
Profit after financial items dropped 36 percent to 1.35 billion crowns in the first six months of the year, and fell below the 1.43 billion crown profit analysts in a Reuter poll had targeted.
The profit was hurt by higher costs, while positive currency effects lifted sales to 18.94 billion crowns from 17.38 billion, Scania said.

Sales of Scania products rose eight percent to 16.64 billion crowns with positive currency effects amounting to 1.1 billion crowns, or 6.5 percent. Adjusted for currency effects, those sales rose somewhat more than one percent.
Operating profit fell to 1.42 billion crowns from 2.29 billion despite positive currency effects of 400 million crowns. The operating margin fell to 7.5 percent from 13.2 percent.
In the second quarter, operating profit rose by 139 million crowns to 781 million crowns from the first quarter, thanks to strong Latin American operations.
Earnings per share dropped to five crowns in the first six months of the year from 7.55 crowns.

In total, Scania sold 22,433 trucks and buses in the first half of 1997, down from 23,012 in the corresponding year-earlier period. In the second quarter, it sold 12,274 trucks and buses, up from 10,159 in the first quarter.
"The six-month result was marked by low sales volumes and continued price pressure in Europe," Scania's chief executive Leif Ostling said in the statement.

"The upturn in demand for heavy trucks which began at the end of the first quarter strengthened during the second quarter. The increased order intake will not show in sales until the second half of 1997. The market seems to be picking up."
Increased demand usually leads to more stable prices, he said, pointing to Latin America where the price and sales volumes trend have been positive.
Scania's Latin American truck deliveries rose 39 percent and order intake, 45 percent.
In Brazil, Scania's single largest market, the company boosted its truck market share to 41.5 percent from 37.5 percent but in Western Europe its market share fell to 15.4 percent from 16.1 percent.
Scania said the Western European bus market remained at the same level as in the first half of 1996, while its market share fell to 8.1 percent in the first five months of the year from 10.1 percent.
Western European order intake for buses rose by 50 percent, mainly because of large successes in Spain. The Latin American bus market was somewhat weaker but orders rose by 20 percent.
